sections.heading: What is levothyroxine used for?
sections.body:
Levothyroxine is a medicine for an underactive thyroid, which is called hypothyroidism. The NHS says it suits most adults and children, though it is not right for everyone, so a clinician checks first.

MedlinePlus, a US source, says it is also used alongside surgery and radioactive iodine treatment for thyroid cancer. It warns that levothyroxine should not be used to lose weight, and that large amounts, especially with amphetamines, can cause serious or life-threatening harm.

sections.heading: How does levothyroxine work, and how long is it taken for?
sections.body:
Levothyroxine is a man-made version of thyroxine, the main hormone the thyroid makes, so it stands in for what an underactive gland is not producing. The NHS says treatment usually carries on for the rest of a person's life. MedlinePlus says people are told to keep taking it even when they feel well, and not to stop without talking to their doctor.

At first there are regular blood tests until the right amount is reached. Once the result is steady, the NHS says a blood test about once a year is usual.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of levothyroxine?
sections.body:
The NHS lists difficulty sleeping, headaches, feeling anxious, sweating and hair loss as the common side effects. It says most side effects happen when the dose is too high, and NHS leaflets describe signs of too much thyroid hormone such as sweating, headaches, diarrhoea and being sick.

Serious side effects are rare. The NHS lists a sudden rise in thyroid hormone, called thyroid crisis, which can cause a high temperature, a fast or irregular heartbeat, dizziness or faintness, and yellowing of the skin or eyes. It also lists a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), with swelling of the throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash or difficulty breathing. For a suspected anaphylactic reaction the NHS says to call 999.

sections.heading: Can levothyroxine be taken with food, drinks or other medicines?
sections.body:
The NHS says levothyroxine is usually taken on an empty stomach, before the first meal of the day, and before any drink with caffeine, such as tea or coffee, or any other medicine. An NHS trust leaflet explains that caffeinated drinks, calcium, iron and antacids can disturb how well the medicine is absorbed.

The NHS page also lists calcium and iron supplements and antidepressants such as sertraline among medicines that can interact with levothyroxine.

sections.heading: Is levothyroxine used in pregnancy and breastfeeding?
sections.body:
The NHS says levothyroxine can be taken in pregnancy if needed. Extra blood tests may be needed to check thyroid hormone levels and that the amount suits the person. A UK hospital leaflet notes that the amount often has to be raised early in pregnancy, and that most women return to their earlier amount after the birth.

The NHS says levothyroxine can usually be taken while breastfeeding, but advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor first.

faqs.q: Will I need levothyroxine for life?
faqs.a: The NHS says treatment for an underactive thyroid usually carries on for the rest of a person's life. Blood tests are used at first to find the right amount, and once the result is steady a yearly check is usual. MedlinePlus says people are told to keep taking it when they feel well and not to stop without speaking to their doctor.

faqs.q: Is levothyroxine used for weight loss?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus, a US source, warns against using levothyroxine to lose weight. It says large amounts, especially taken with amphetamines, can cause serious or life-threatening harm. The medicine is prescribed to replace a missing hormone, and the dose is checked with blood tests.

faqs.q: What happens if a dose is missed or too much is taken?
faqs.a: The NHS says a missed dose is taken once remembered, unless the next one is nearly due, in which case the missed one is skipped. It advises against taking two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. A Sheffield Children's leaflet says an extra dose given to a child by mistake is unlikely to cause harm. For taking more than prescribed, the NHS says to speak to a pharmacist as soon as possible, or call NHS 111 if none can be reached or the extra was taken on purpose.

faqs.q: Do other medicines or supplements affect levothyroxine?
faqs.a: Some can. An NHS trust leaflet says calcium, iron and antacids can disturb absorption, and the NHS page lists calcium and iron supplements and antidepressants such as sertraline among those to be aware of. A pharmacist or doctor can check any new medicine, supplement or herbal product against levothyroxine.

faqs.q: What tests are used while taking levothyroxine?
faqs.a: Blood tests are used to check that the amount suits the person, and the results guide any change. Once the result is stable the NHS says a yearly test is usual.

sections.heading: What is salbutamol used for?
sections.body:
Salbutamol is a reliever inhaler, the kind many people know as the blue inhaler. The NHS describes it as a medicine that makes breathing easier when asthma or other breathing conditions cause wheezing and breathlessness. It is also used for symptoms of long-term lung conditions such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

According to the NHS, a reliever works quickly to ease symptoms, and people with asthma are also given a preventer inhaler that is used every day to help stop symptoms. The NHS adds that keeping a diary of how often the reliever is used helps when talking about asthma or COPD control with a doctor or nurse.

sections.heading: How does a salbutamol inhaler work?
sections.body:
Salbutamol is a bronchodilator, which means it relaxes the muscles around the airways so they widen. The NHS says it works almost straight away after a puff and keeps working for a few hours.

Pressurised (metered-dose) inhalers, sometimes called puffers, contain hydrofluorocarbon propellants, while dry powder inhalers do not. The NHS says a person may be asked whether switching to a more environmentally friendly inhaler would suit them.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of salbutamol?
sections.body:
The NHS describes salbutamol as very effective with few side effects when it is used properly. Common side effects, which the NHS says affect more than 1 in 100 people, are feeling shaky, a faster heartbeat and headaches. Salbutamol can also cause dizziness or shakiness, and the NHS advises not to drive, cycle or use tools or machinery until feeling better.

Using too much can make the heart beat faster than normal and cause shakiness. The NHS says to contact NHS 111 about a fast or noticeably pounding heartbeat after using too much, and to call 999 if there is chest pain. Serious side effects are rare. The NHS lists muscle pain or weakness, muscle cramps, a fast irregular heartbeat that does not settle, and very bad dizziness as warning signs, and it says new or worsening breathlessness or chest pain needs a 999 call or a trip to A&E. A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is also possible. Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue is one sign, and it needs an emergency 999 call.

sections.heading: Can I drink alcohol or take salbutamol with other medicines?
sections.body:
The NHS says alcohol is fine and normal eating and drinking can continue while using a salbutamol inhaler. It does not affect contraception, including the combined pill and emergency contraception.

Salbutamol can generally be used with most medicines, but some combinations need care. The NHS says water tablets (diuretics), steroid tablets such as prednisolone, and theophylline or aminophylline can raise the risk of low potassium, and it names beta blockers as another combination that can cause problems. The NHS also says there is not enough information on how herbal remedies and supplements interact with salbutamol, and it advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor before starting any new medicine, herbal remedy or supplement.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with salbutamol, and is it used in pregnancy?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults and children can use salbutamol inhalers. Extra advice is suggested for people who have had an allergy to salbutamol or other medicines, or who have heart problems, an overactive thyroid, low potassium in the blood or diabetes.

The NHS says salbutamol can be used in pregnancy, and stresses the importance of keeping asthma under control. For breastfeeding, the NHS says the inhaler can be used as normal. It says the amount reaching breast milk is not known but is likely to be very low, and that it has been used this way for many years without side effects in babies. The NHS also says there is no evidence that salbutamol affects fertility in men or women.

sections.heading: What if I need my inhaler more often or have an asthma attack?
sections.body:
The NHS says that needing salbutamol more often than usual can mean a condition is getting worse, and it advises speaking to a doctor, pharmacist or nurse.

For an asthma attack, the NHS says to call 999 if breathing does not improve after using the reliever inhaler. Asthma and Lung UK says to call 999 if the reliever is not helping or the person feels worse at any point, and that calling an ambulance means treatment can start on the way to hospital. After an attack that was managed with the reliever alone, Asthma and Lung UK advises asking for an urgent same-day appointment with a GP or nurse.

faqs.q: Does using a salbutamol inhaler for many years cause harm?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no evidence that salbutamol does any lasting damage to the body, even if it is used for many years. Needing it more often than usual can be a sign that a condition is getting worse, and the NHS advises speaking to a doctor, pharmacist or nurse about that.

faqs.q: Can I drive after using my blue inhaler?
faqs.a: The NHS says salbutamol can cause dizziness or shakiness in some people. If that happens, it advises not to drive, cycle or use tools or machinery until feeling better, and says that anyone in doubt should not drive.

faqs.q: What happens if I use too much salbutamol?
faqs.a: Using too much can make the heart beat faster than normal and cause shakiness. The NHS says to contact NHS 111 about a fast or noticeably pounding heartbeat after using too much, and to call 999 if there is chest pain.

faqs.q: Does salbutamol affect contraception?
faqs.a: According to the NHS, salbutamol does not affect any type of contraception. This includes the combined pill and emergency contraception. The NHS also says alcohol is fine and normal eating and drinking can continue while using the inhaler.

faqs.q: Is salbutamol an emergency treatment?
faqs.a: The reliever inhaler is what the NHS and Asthma and Lung UK describe using during an asthma attack. The NHS says that if breathing does not improve after using it, a 999 call is needed. Needing it more often than usual is a reason to speak to a doctor, pharmacist or nurse.

sections.heading: What is warfarin used for, and how is it monitored?
sections.body:
Warfarin is an anticoagulant, often called a blood thinner, used to prevent and treat blood clots. It does not literally thin the blood; it makes clots form less readily. Because it lowers the chance of clots, the main risk that comes with it is bleeding.

People taking warfarin are given an anticoagulant alert card. Regular blood tests measure how quickly the blood clots, and the result guides the warfarin dose. This test is called the international normalised ratio, or INR. Testing is usually more frequent while the right dose is being found.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of warfarin?
sections.body:
The main side effect of warfarin is an increased risk of bleeding. The NHS lists blood in the urine or poo, unexplained bruising or nosebleeds, and coughing up or vomiting blood among the signs of bleeding.

The NHS says to get urgent advice from NHS 111 if there are signs of bleeding, after a head injury, or if another serious side effect is suspected. Severe bleeding that will not stop needs a 999 call or A&E. A sudden bad headache with confusion, slurred speech or difficulty moving the arms or legs can signal bleeding in the brain, which is an emergency needing a 999 call.

A painful skin rash can be a sign of a rare condition called calciphylaxis. A severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is an emergency needing a 999 call. Both are listed on the NHS page.

sections.heading: Can I eat and drink what I like on warfarin?
sections.body:
Foods rich in vitamin K, such as leafy greens, affect how warfarin works. The NHS says they can still be eaten; keeping the amount steady matters more than avoiding them, and the warfarin clinic can adjust the dose to match. Cranberry juice and grapefruit juice are best avoided because they can increase the blood-thinning effect.

The NHS advises never binge drinking on warfarin, and keeping regular drinking modest.

sections.heading: Can I take other medicines, supplements or herbal remedies with warfarin?
sections.body: The NHS says some medicines, remedies and supplements may not mix well with warfarin, so a doctor should know about everything else a person takes. Painkillers such as ibuprofen, antibiotics, antidepressants and statins are among the medicines the NHS lists as possible problems. The NHS advises against St John's wort and vitamin K supplements while on warfarin. Illness with sickness or diarrhoea can change how warfarin works, so the anticoagulant clinic is told about illness as well as new medicines.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with warfarin, and what about pregnancy?
sections.body:
The NHS says most people can take warfarin, but it is not suitable for everyone. It lists an allergy to warfarin, liver or kidney problems, a recent stroke, recent or planned surgery, and a condition that makes bleeding more likely.

Warfarin is not usually used in pregnancy because it can affect the baby's development, though it is sometimes used after the doctor discusses risks and benefits. The NHS advises anyone who is pregnant or planning a pregnancy to speak to their GP or anticoagulant clinic, and not to stop warfarin unless a doctor says so. The NHS says warfarin can usually be taken while breastfeeding, after discussing it with a GP or midwife first.

faqs.q: Does warfarin really thin the blood?
faqs.a: Not literally; it is called a blood thinner, but it makes clots form less readily. The NHS describes it as a medicine used to prevent and treat blood clots, and says its main side effect is an increased risk of bleeding.

faqs.q: What is an anticoagulant alert card?
faqs.a: It is a card given to people taking warfarin, who may be at risk of bleeding.

faqs.q: What should be done after a head injury on warfarin?
faqs.a: The NHS says to get urgent advice from NHS 111 after a head injury while on warfarin, as well as for any signs of bleeding. A sudden bad headache with confusion, slurred speech or difficulty moving the arms or legs can signal bleeding in the brain and needs a 999 call.

faqs.q: Do I have to avoid green vegetables on warfarin?
faqs.a: No. Leafy greens are rich in vitamin K and affect warfarin, but the NHS says they can still be eaten and that a steady intake matters, so the clinic can adjust the dose. Cranberry juice and grapefruit juice are the drinks to avoid.

faqs.q: Can warfarin be taken in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says warfarin is not usually used in pregnancy because it can affect the baby's development, although it is sometimes used after the doctor talks through risks and benefits. Anyone pregnant or planning a pregnancy is advised to speak to their GP or anticoagulant clinic and not to stop it unless a doctor says so.

sections.heading: What is apixaban used for?
sections.body:
Apixaban is an anticoagulant, a medicine that helps prevent blood clots from forming. It is available in the UK only on prescription.

The NHS says it is used to treat blood clots in the veins, such as deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and in the lungs, called pulmonary embolism. It is also given to people at high risk of clots, such as those with atrial fibrillation (an irregular heartbeat), heart failure, or a past stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA). It is also given after a recent hip or knee replacement.

sections.heading: How does apixaban work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
Apixaban makes the blood take longer to clot, which lowers the chance of a harmful clot but also means bleeding can last longer. The tablets can be taken with or without food.

The NHS says a person should not stop apixaban without talking to their doctor. If it is stopped, the way the blood clots goes back to what it was before treatment, usually within a day or two. The NHS gives missed-dose advice on its anticoagulant dosage page; it depends on how long it is until the next scheduled dose.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of apixaban?
sections.body:
The most common side effect is bleeding more easily than normal. This can show as nosebleeds, bleeding gums, bruising or heavier periods. The NHS describes this kind of bleeding as not dangerous, and says it should stop by itself. The doctor should be told if it bothers the person or does not stop.

The NHS lists blood in urine or stools, and coughing up or vomiting blood, among the more serious effects. On its main apixaban page, the NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding, a head injury, or other possible serious side effects.

Very rarely, apixaban can cause bleeding in the brain. On its side-effects page the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a sudden severe headache unlike any before, fits, sudden loss of vision or blurred vision, or numbness or tingling in the arms or legs. The two NHS pages are worded differently: the main page names NHS 111 for bleeding and head injury, and the side-effects page names 999 or A&E for these brain-bleed signs.

A serious allergic reaction, such as swelling of the face or throat or difficulty breathing, is a reason to call 999.

sections.heading: Can I take other medicines or drink alcohol with apixaban?
sections.body:
The NHS says some medicines may not mix well with apixaban, including other anticoagulants, some antidepressants, and painkillers or anti-inflammatories such as aspirin and ibuprofen. The NHS says not to take aspirin or ibuprofen unless a doctor has said it is fine, as they raise the chance of bleeding.

The NHS asks people to tell their doctor, dentist or pharmacist about every medicine they take, including over-the-counter medicines, vitamins and herbal supplements. It names St John's wort, a herbal remedy for low mood, as one to avoid. It also says there is not enough information to say that other herbal remedies and supplements are safe to take with apixaban.

The NHS says it is possible to drink alcohol while taking apixaban, but heavy or binge drinking raises the risk of bleeding.

sections.heading: Apixaban, surgery and the alert card
sections.body: The NHS says people taking apixaban should carry an anticoagulant alert card and tell their surgeon or dentist that they take it. Because of the risk of bleeding, the dose may need to be lowered or stopped a few days before an operation, and the clinical team makes that decision.

sections.heading: Who may not be able to take apixaban?
sections.body:
The NHS lists reasons apixaban may not be suitable, including a past allergic reaction to apixaban or any other medicine, active heavy bleeding, a stomach ulcer, a recent bleed in the brain, and liver or kidney problems.

The NHS says apixaban can be harmful to a baby, so pregnancy or trying to become pregnant is on its list of reasons. It also says apixaban should not be used while breastfeeding.

faqs.q: Is apixaban an anticoagulant?
faqs.a: Yes. The NHS describes apixaban as an anticoagulant that helps prevent blood clots. It is only available on prescription in the UK.

faqs.q: What does the NHS say about a missed apixaban tablet?
faqs.a: The NHS gives missed-dose advice on its anticoagulant dosage page. It depends on how long it is until the next scheduled dose, and this site does not give the timings.

faqs.q: Can apixaban be stopped if someone feels fine?
faqs.a: The NHS says not to stop apixaban without talking to the doctor first. If it is stopped, the way the blood clots returns to what it was before treatment, usually within a day or two.

faqs.q: What does the NHS say about a head injury or bleeding on apixaban?
faqs.a: On its main apixaban page, the NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding, a head injury or other possible serious side effects. On its side-effects page, it says to call 999 or go to A&E for a sudden severe headache, fits, or sudden vision changes.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk while taking apixaban?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is possible to drink alcohol while taking apixaban. Heavy or binge drinking raises the risk of bleeding.

sections.heading: What is citalopram used for?
sections.body:
The NHS describes citalopram as an antidepressant that is often used to treat low mood and depression. It is also sometimes used for panic attacks. It belongs to a group of antidepressants called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs.

For citalopram, the NHS says people usually need to take it for at least 6 months, and to keep taking it for as long as the doctor recommends. The NHS does not usually recommend citalopram for children and young people under 18.

sections.heading: How long does it take to work, and what about stopping?
sections.body:
The NHS says it may take one or two weeks before citalopram starts to work on symptoms, and it usually takes between four and six weeks before the full benefit is felt. The NHS advises giving it at least six weeks, and talking to the doctor if there is no improvement after six weeks. If side effects continue, the NHS says a different type of antidepressant may be needed.

The NHS says citalopram should not be stopped suddenly or without talking to the doctor first, because this may cause withdrawal symptoms. If the person and the doctor decide to stop, the doctor may recommend reducing the amount gradually, which the NHS describes as usually over several weeks, or longer after a long course. The NHS lists feeling dizzy, feeling sick, trouble sleeping, feeling agitated or anxious, and headaches among possible withdrawal symptoms.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of citalopram?
sections.body:
The NHS describes common side effects as ones that affect more than 1 in 100 people. Examples it gives include headaches, sweating, dry mouth and sleep problems. It says these are usually mild and most ease after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine.

The NHS also lists sexual side effects, such as a lower sex drive and erection or orgasm problems. It says these can sometimes be long lasting and may not get better even after the medicine is stopped.

The NHS calls serious side effects rare, affecting fewer than 1 in 1,000 people. They include a severe allergic reaction, and serotonin syndrome, a rare but serious condition that causes a fast heartbeat, sweating, shaking, twitching muscles, and feeling confused or agitated. They also include a rare, life-threatening heart rhythm problem that causes a fast, irregular heartbeat, light-headedness and fainting. The NHS says bleeding from the gums, unexplained bruising, or blood in the urine or stools is a reason to speak to a doctor or call NHS 111.

sections.heading: Where to get urgent help
sections.body:
The NHS says to call NHS 111 if someone taking citalopram thinks they may be having serious side effects. It says to call 999 or go to A&E for chest pain or pressure, a fit or seizure for the first time, or feeling very dizzy or passing out. Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue also needs a 999 call, according to the NHS.

For thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, the NHS says to call 999 or go straight to A&E if you think you may be about to harm yourself, or if you already have. The NHS also suggests calling NHS 111 or using its online service to find support. Samaritans can be reached free, at any time and from any phone, on 116 123. The charity Mind says that if you have suicidal feelings while taking medication, you can contact your GP as soon as possible, or speak to a pharmacist or NHS 111.

sections.heading: Can you take citalopram with other medicines or alcohol?
sections.body:
The NHS advises not using St John's wort, a herbal remedy, with citalopram because it increases the risk of side effects. It says other herbal remedies and supplements are not tested in the same way as pharmacy and prescription medicines, and are generally not tested for their effect on other medicines. The NHS advises telling the doctor or pharmacist about any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

The NHS says using citalopram with other medicines can increase the chance of side effects. Its list includes sumatriptan, strong painkillers such as tramadol, anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), blood thinners, medicines that affect heart rhythm and other antidepressants.

On alcohol, the NHS says it may make a person feel sleepy, and that it might be best to stop drinking alcohol until they see how the medicine makes them feel.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what about pregnancy and breastfeeding?
sections.body:
The NHS lists a heart condition, such as a heart rhythm problem, among the reasons citalopram may not suit some people.

According to the NHS, citalopram can be used in pregnancy if needed. The doctor will talk through the risks and benefits and prescribe the lowest effective amount. The NHS says some studies have suggested citalopram might occasionally affect a baby's heart development, but that if there is any risk it is small, and most babies born to women taking it have a normal heart. Taking it in the last month of pregnancy may slightly increase the risk of bleeding after delivery.

If the doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy, the NHS says citalopram can be taken while breastfeeding. It passes into breast milk in fairly small amounts, and the NHS says it is important to continue taking it to keep the mother well.

faqs.q: How long does citalopram take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says citalopram may start to work on symptoms after one or two weeks. The full benefit usually takes four to six weeks. If there is no improvement after about six weeks, the NHS advises talking to the doctor.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on citalopram?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol may make a person feel sleepy while taking citalopram. It says it might be best to stop drinking alcohol until they see how the medicine makes them feel.

faqs.q: Can citalopram be stopped suddenly?
faqs.a: The NHS says it should not be stopped suddenly, because this may cause withdrawal symptoms. If the person and the doctor decide to stop, the doctor may recommend reducing the amount gradually. The NHS lists feeling dizzy, feeling sick, trouble sleeping, feeling agitated or anxious, and headaches among possible withdrawal symptoms.

faqs.q: Is citalopram used in pregnancy and breastfeeding?
faqs.a: According to the NHS, citalopram can be used in pregnancy if needed, at the lowest effective amount. Taking it in the last month of pregnancy may slightly increase the risk of bleeding after delivery. It can be taken while breastfeeding if the doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy.

faqs.q: What should happen if someone has thoughts of harming themselves?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 or go straight to A&E if you think you may be about to harm yourself, or if you already have. Samaritans can be reached free on 116 123 at any time. Mind says that if you have suicidal feelings while taking medication, you can contact your GP as soon as possible, or speak to a pharmacist or NHS 111. For other serious side effects, the NHS says to call NHS 111.

sections.heading: What is losartan used for?
sections.body: Losartan is a medicine for high blood pressure, and it belongs to the group called angiotensin II receptor blockers. The NHS says it can also be used to treat heart failure and for kidney problems in people with diabetes, where it helps to protect the kidneys. It is available on prescription only.

sections.heading: How does losartan work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
Losartan blocks the effect of a hormone called angiotensin II, which narrows blood vessels. The NHS says that, like other medicines in this group, losartan relaxes and widens the blood vessels, which lowers blood pressure and makes it easier for the heart to pump blood around the body.

The NHS says losartan can be taken with or without food, and that it should not be stopped unless a doctor says so, even when a person feels well.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of losartan?
sections.body:
The NHS lists dizziness, tiredness, headache, tummy pain, feeling or being sick, and swelling of the legs, ankles or feet as common side effects. It says losartan can make people feel dizzy, especially when they first start taking it or after a bigger dose, and that anyone who feels dizzy should not drive, ride a bike, or use tools or machinery until they feel better.

Taking losartan for a long time can sometimes mean the kidneys do not work as well as they should, so the doctor checks kidney function with regular blood tests. The NHS says yellow skin or yellow whites of the eyes may be a sign of liver problems, and that this can be harder to see on brown or black skin. For this, the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away. It also lists feeling weak, an irregular heartbeat, pins and needles and muscle cramps as possible signs of changes in blood potassium, with the same advice to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away.

sections.heading: What are the signs of a serious allergic reaction or swelling?
sections.body: A serious allergic reaction to losartan is rare. The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if breathing becomes difficult, and not to drive to A&E. A raised, itchy rash can also be part of an allergic reaction. Sudden swelling of parts of the body is called angioedema, and the NHS lists a past episode of it as a reason losartan may not be suitable.

sections.heading: Can losartan be taken with other medicines, alcohol or potassium salt substitutes?
sections.body:
The NHS lists painkillers such as ibuprofen, naproxen and diclofenac among the medicines that do not mix well with losartan. It also lists other blood pressure medicines, diuretics, lithium and heparin. A pharmacist or doctor can be asked about any combination.

The NHS advises against potassium-rich salt substitutes such as LoSalt, because they may push the level of potassium in the blood too high when mixed with losartan. Alcohol can add to the blood pressure lowering effect of losartan and may bring on dizziness or light-headedness. The NHS advises limiting alcohol while taking it, because alcohol can increase the risk of side effects.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with losartan, including in pregnancy and during illness?
sections.body:
The NHS says losartan is not recommended in pregnancy, because it can reduce the fluid around the baby, particularly in the second and third trimesters. It advises women who could become pregnant to use contraception while taking it and to plan any pregnancy with their doctor. For breastfeeding, the NHS says to talk to a doctor or pharmacist first.

The NHS says losartan may not be suitable for people with a history of angioedema or with liver problems. It also says vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration, and that a doctor or pharmacist may recommend stopping losartan until the person is better.

faqs.q: What are the common side effects of losartan?
faqs.a: The common side effects the NHS lists for losartan are dizziness, tiredness, headache, tummy pain, feeling or being sick, and swelling of the legs, ankles or feet.

faqs.q: What should happen if the lips or tongue swell while taking losartan?
faqs.a: Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue is treated as an emergency. The NHS says to call 999, and not to drive to A&E oneself. Past angioedema, meaning earlier sudden swelling of this kind, is also a reason losartan may not be suitable for a person.

faqs.q: Can painkillers like ibuprofen be taken with losartan?
faqs.a: The NHS lists painkillers such as ibuprofen, naproxen and diclofenac among the medicines that do not mix well with losartan. It also lists other blood pressure medicines among those that can interact.

faqs.q: Does alcohol affect losartan?
faqs.a: Alcohol can add to the blood pressure lowering effect of losartan. That may lead to dizziness or light-headedness. During the first few days of taking it, or after a bigger dose, the NHS says it is best to avoid alcohol until it is clear how the medicine affects the person.

sections.heading: What is lisinopril used for?
sections.body:
Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor. The NHS says it is used to treat high blood pressure, a recent heart attack and kidney problems caused by diabetes, and it is also used with other medicines for heart failure. The NHS says most adults and children aged 6 years and over can take it.

For high blood pressure, heart failure and kidney disease caused by diabetes, treatment is usually long term and can continue for the rest of a person's life. The NHS says stopping lisinopril may cause blood pressure to rise, so it advises speaking to a doctor before stopping.

sections.heading: How does lisinopril work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
Lisinopril widens the blood vessels, which lowers blood pressure. The NHS says blood pressure can start to fall within hours, but the full effect may take a few weeks. In heart failure, improvement can take weeks or even months, and a lack of obvious change does not mean the medicine is not working.

The NHS says the tablets are swallowed whole with a drink of water, with or without food, and suggests taking them at the same time each day. The amount usually starts low and is increased gradually, and a doctor may suggest taking the first one before bedtime because it can cause dizziness.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of lisinopril?
sections.body:
The NHS lists these common side effects: headaches, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, dizziness (especially on standing up quickly) and a dry cough that does not go away. Kidney problems are also listed as common, and blood tests can check for them. Dizziness is most likely when starting lisinopril or moving to a higher dose. The cough may take up to a month to clear after the medicine is stopped.

If a side effect such as the cough makes lisinopril hard to take, the NHS says a different type of blood pressure medicine may be possible. Because stopping may cause blood pressure to rise, it advises speaking to a doctor first.

Serious side effects are rare. The NHS says sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or struggling to breathe, can be signs of a serious allergic reaction, and it says to call 999 for these. It also lists yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes, which can point to liver problems and may be harder to see on brown or black skin, and swollen ankles, blood in the pee or passing very little pee, which can point to kidney problems. For these, the NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111.

sections.heading: Can lisinopril be taken with other medicines, alcohol or salt substitutes?
sections.body:
The NHS says alcohol can make the blood-pressure-lowering effect stronger and cause dizziness or light-headedness. It advises avoiding alcohol during the first few days of treatment or after an increase, until it is clear how the medicine affects a person.

The NHS says not to use salt substitutes such as Lo-Salt, because they are high in potassium and may push the potassium level in the blood too high. Its list of medicines to be careful with also includes other medicines that raise potassium, such as spironolactone, triamterene, amiloride, potassium supplements, trimethoprim and heparin. The list also includes anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, indomethacin and aspirin; the NHS says low-dose aspirin can be taken with lisinopril.

The NHS says to contact a doctor if there is a high temperature, sweats, shaking, or severe diarrhoea or vomiting. The doctor may tell the person to pause lisinopril until they recover.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with lisinopril, and what about pregnancy and breastfeeding?
sections.body:
The NHS lists groups who may not be able to take lisinopril, including people who have had an allergic reaction to it or another medicine. It also lists people with heart, liver or kidney problems, diabetes, unstable or low blood pressure, and those having dialysis.

The NHS says lisinopril is not recommended in pregnancy. Its main concern is the baby's kidneys and lungs, particularly if it is taken in the second and third trimesters, and it says lisinopril should be stopped by 12 weeks of pregnancy at the latest. If someone is already pregnant, the NHS advises talking to a doctor as soon as possible, and says a different medicine can usually be prescribed.

For breastfeeding, the NHS says it might be OK to take lisinopril but to talk to a doctor or pharmacist first. The UK manufacturer leaflet is more cautious and says lisinopril is not recommended for mothers who are breastfeeding, and that a doctor may choose another treatment.

faqs.q: Does lisinopril cause a cough, and does it go away?
faqs.a: A dry cough that does not go away is one of the common side effects of lisinopril. The NHS says cough medicines do not usually help and that it can take up to a month to clear after the medicine is stopped. If the cough prevents someone taking lisinopril, a different type of blood pressure medicine may be possible, but the NHS advises speaking to a doctor before stopping because blood pressure may rise.

faqs.q: What are the signs of a serious allergic reaction or angioedema?
faqs.a: Angioedema is swelling of the lips, tongue and face. The NHS says sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or struggling to breathe, can be signs of a serious allergic reaction, and it says to call 999. The NHS also says the chance of angioedema is higher for people with black skin.

faqs.q: Can salt substitutes or painkillers such as ibuprofen be used with lisinopril?
faqs.a: The NHS says not to use salt substitutes such as Lo-Salt, because they are high in potassium and may push the potassium level in the blood too high. It also lists anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, indomethacin and aspirin among medicines to be careful with, and says low-dose aspirin can be taken with lisinopril.

faqs.q: Can lisinopril be taken in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says lisinopril is not recommended in pregnancy, mainly because of effects on the baby's kidneys and lungs, and that it should be stopped by 12 weeks at the latest. It says a doctor can usually prescribe a different medicine. For breastfeeding, the NHS says it might be OK but to talk to a doctor or pharmacist first, while the UK manufacturer leaflet says it is not recommended for breastfeeding mothers.

sections.heading: What is bisoprolol used for?
sections.body:
Bisoprolol is a beta blocker, a type of medicine used to treat high blood pressure and heart failure. It is also used to prevent the chest pain caused by angina, and to treat atrial fibrillation and other conditions that cause an irregular heartbeat. It is only available on prescription.

The NHS says bisoprolol works as well as other beta blockers at lowering blood pressure but is less likely to cause side effects, because it acts mainly on the heart. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) calls this kind of beta blocker selective, meaning it mostly blocks the effects of adrenaline and noradrenaline in the heart, with less effect on other parts of the body. Manufacturer leaflets say it is not recommended for children or adolescents.

sections.heading: How does bisoprolol work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
The BHF explains that beta blockers slow the heart rate and reduce how hard the heart has to work. They do this by blocking the effects of the stress hormones adrenaline and noradrenaline, which make the heart work harder and faster.

The NHS says bisoprolol tablets are swallowed with a drink of water and can be taken with or without food. It says treatment is usually long term, and that the very first dose can make some people feel dizzy. Doses differ between people and conditions, so none are given here. If someone feels dizzy or weak, the NHS advises stopping what they are doing and sitting or lying down until they feel better.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of bisoprolol?
sections.body:
The NHS lists headaches, tiredness, cold or tingly hands and feet, dizziness from low blood pressure, feeling or being sick, and diarrhoea or constipation as common side effects. They usually happen when treatment starts or when the amount is increased, and they often get better over time.

Serious side effects are uncommon. The NHS lists a serious allergic reaction, liver inflammation, breathing problems, and an irregular heartbeat or worsening heart failure symptoms. For a serious allergic reaction, the NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if breathing is very fast or hard. It says to call a doctor or NHS 111 if the whites of the eyes or the skin turn yellow, which can be a sign of liver problems.

sections.heading: Is it dangerous to stop bisoprolol suddenly?
sections.body:
The NHS says people still get the benefits of bisoprolol when they feel well. It advises talking to a doctor if you want to stop, because stopping can make blood pressure rise, which raises the risk of heart attack and stroke.

Manufacturer leaflets say that if bisoprolol is suddenly stopped, side effects are likely, and that treatment should not be stopped abruptly. Leaflets describe the amount being reduced gradually, and they say to speak to the prescriber before stopping.

sections.heading: Taking bisoprolol with other medicines or alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says some medicines can interact with bisoprolol. Other medicines that lower blood pressure can sometimes push it too low, which may cause dizziness or fainting. Painkillers such as ibuprofen can make bisoprolol less effective. The NHS page also flags some decongestants and cold remedies, and medicines for asthma, COPD and diabetes. It says its list is not complete.

For herbal remedies and supplements the NHS says there is very little information, and it advises telling a doctor or pharmacist about any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

On alcohol, the NHS says it is best to avoid drinking when first starting bisoprolol or when the amount is increased, until you see how the medicine affects you. It also says alcohol will make dizziness or weakness feel worse.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with bisoprolol?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults aged 18 and over can take bisoprolol, but it is not suitable for everyone. It lists a previous allergic reaction to bisoprolol or another medicine, low blood pressure, a slow heart rate, worsening heart failure, heart disease, a recent heart attack, severe circulation problems, metabolic acidosis, and lung disease or severe asthma among the reasons to check with a doctor first. Manufacturer leaflets also list severe asthma and an untreated tumour of the adrenal gland called phaeochromocytoma as reasons not to take it. Bisoprolol may make the warning signs of low blood sugar harder to recognise.

The NHS says bisoprolol can be taken during pregnancy, but the mother and baby may be offered extra checks. Its pregnancy page says it can sometimes affect a baby's growth, so extra ultrasound scans may be needed. Taking it while breastfeeding may cause side effects in the baby, although a doctor may still recommend it if the benefits outweigh the risks. One UK product leaflet advises against use in pregnancy, which differs from the NHS advice.

faqs.q: Does bisoprolol make you tired?
faqs.a: The NHS lists tiredness as a common side effect of bisoprolol. Common side effects usually happen when treatment starts or the amount is increased, and they often get better over time. If someone feels dizzy or weak, the NHS advice is to stop what they are doing and sit or lie down until they feel better.

faqs.q: Can I stop taking bisoprolol if I feel fine?
faqs.a: The NHS says people still get the benefits of bisoprolol when they feel well, and that stopping can make blood pressure rise, raising the risk of heart attack and stroke. Leaflets say stopping suddenly is likely to cause side effects and that the amount is reduced gradually. The NHS advises talking to a doctor before stopping.

faqs.q: Does bisoprolol cause breathing problems?
faqs.a: The NHS lists breathing problems among the serious side effects of bisoprolol, which are uncommon. It says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, or if breathing is very fast or hard. The NHS also lists lung disease or severe asthma among the conditions to check with a doctor before taking it.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking bisoprolol?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is best to avoid alcohol when first starting bisoprolol or when the amount is increased, until you see how it affects you. It also says alcohol will make dizziness or weakness feel worse.

faqs.q: Is bisoprolol the same as other beta blockers?
faqs.a: Bisoprolol is one of several beta blockers. The NHS says it works as well as others for lowering blood pressure but is less likely to cause side effects because it acts mainly on the heart. The BHF says selective beta blockers mostly block adrenaline and noradrenaline in the heart, while non-selective ones also block them in other parts of the body.

sections.heading: What is tramadol used for?
sections.body:
Tramadol belongs to a group of medicines called opioids. The NHS describes it as a strong painkiller used to treat moderate to severe pain. A doctor may also prescribe it for severe pain when weaker painkillers do not help.

The NHS says standard forms usually start to ease pain within about 30 to 60 minutes, and the relief wears off after 4 to 6 hours. Slow-release forms take longer to start working but last longer. Tramadol also raises serotonin levels in the brain, which is why it can interact with certain antidepressants and other medicines.

sections.heading: What happens if too much is taken?
sections.body: The NHS lists warning signs of taking too much: feeling very sleepy, sick or dizzy, difficulty breathing, and becoming unconscious. It says the amount that can lead to an overdose is different for everyone, and that help should be sought immediately if too much may have been taken. The NHS also says slow-release tablets are swallowed whole, because breaking, crushing, chewing or sucking them can cause an overdose.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of tramadol?
sections.body:
The NHS says common side effects, which affect more than 1 in 100 people, include headaches, feeling or being sick, constipation, dry mouth, sweating, and feeling sleepy or dizzy. Not everyone gets them.

The NHS says to call 999 for a seizure (fit), breathing difficulties, or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as facial swelling or trouble breathing. It says to call 111 or a doctor for dizziness or weakness (which can be a sign of low blood pressure), hallucinations, confusion, or difficulty passing urine.

A Royal Devon NHS leaflet says that anyone with symptoms of serotonin toxicity should not take the next dose and should seek urgent medical help. The NHS warns that using MDMA (ecstasy), cocaine, amphetamines or LSD with tramadol, or taking it with certain antidepressants, raises the risk of serotonin syndrome.

sections.heading: Can you become addicted to tramadol, and what is withdrawal like?
sections.body:
The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to tramadol. Signs include finding it hard to stop or feeling the need to take it more often than necessary. Long-term use can also lead to tolerance, meaning higher doses are gradually needed to control pain. Stopping can bring on withdrawal symptoms.

A Royal Devon NHS leaflet advises against stopping tramadol suddenly and says anyone who wants to stop should discuss it with a doctor or pharmacist. The NHS says that people who have taken tramadol for more than a few weeks should speak to a doctor before stopping, and that a treatment plan may set out how and when to stop.

sections.heading: Can tramadol be taken with other medicines, alcohol or when driving?
sections.body:
The NHS asks people to tell their doctor about any other medicines they take, including ones for depression or other mental health problems, pain, sleep, anxiety, allergy, blood clots or infection. Prescribing guidance from an NHS trust says tramadol should not be given to people taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), a type of antidepressant. The NHS says carbamazepine, buprenorphine, ondansetron and rifampicin can weaken or shorten the effect of tramadol, and that products containing codeine, including some over-the-counter combinations such as co-codamol, are best avoided. MedlinePlus, a US source, says St John's wort and tryptophan may interact with tramadol. The NHS says there is very little information on taking herbal remedies or supplements with it.

The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol with tramadol because side effects such as sleepiness are more likely. It also says not to drive, cycle or use tools or machinery if tramadol makes a person sleepy, dizzy or clumsy, or if they have blurred vision or cannot concentrate.

sections.heading: Who may not be able to take tramadol, and what about pregnancy or breastfeeding?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults and children aged 12 and over can take tramadol. It lists groups who may not be able to take it, including people who have had an allergic reaction to tramadol or other medicines, and people with a seizure or fit condition, a head injury, breathing difficulties, kidney or liver problems, or an addiction to alcohol, strong painkillers or recreational drugs.

The NHS says tramadol is not known to cause problems with a baby's development, but more studies are needed to confirm this. If it is taken near the end of pregnancy, the baby might have withdrawal symptoms after birth. For breastfeeding, the NHS says tramadol passes into breast milk in very small amounts and is unlikely to cause side effects in the baby. The NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service says it can be used short term with caution and monitoring of the infant, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, and that babies under 2 months are most at risk. Some other NHS leaflets advise against it while breastfeeding, so the decision rests with a doctor or pharmacist.

faqs.q: Is tramadol addictive?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to tramadol. Signs include finding it hard to stop or feeling the need to take it more often than necessary. Stopping can bring withdrawal symptoms. The NHS says people who have taken it for more than a few weeks should speak to a doctor before stopping.

faqs.q: When should someone call 999 about tramadol?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 for a seizure, breathing difficulties, or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as facial swelling or trouble breathing. For dizziness or weakness, hallucinations, confusion or difficulty passing urine, it says to call 111 or a doctor.

faqs.q: Why does tramadol interact with antidepressants?
faqs.a: Tramadol raises serotonin levels in the brain, so combining it with certain antidepressants raises the risk of serotonin syndrome, the NHS says. NHS trust prescribing guidance says it should not be given to people taking MAOI antidepressants.

faqs.q: Can you drink alcohol or drive while taking tramadol?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol with tramadol because side effects such as sleepiness are more likely. It says not to drive, cycle or use tools or machinery if the medicine makes a person sleepy, dizzy or clumsy.
